title: How this 18-year-old’s love of origami helped him win a $100,000 at a science fair
excerpt: Hikaru Kuribayashi used origami-inspired technology to win a $100,000 prize at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair in May.
content_html:
By Lauren Edmonds

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Growing up on Japan's northernmost island allowed Hikaru Kuribayashi to immerse himself in nature, where origami patterns are everywhere.

"Imagine a tiny ladybug," Kuribayashi, 18, told Business Insider. "That ladybug actually uses origami patterns to fold and expand its wings."

Leaves. Flower petals. Insect wings. He'd often notice the intricate patterns while traversing the Hokkaido prefecture's sprawling forests and mountains. Kuribayashi, however, believed origami's influence on nature could reach beyond artistic inspiration.

"Origami and linkages have been used in many, many other fields," Kuribayashi said. "For example, some satellites in orbit use origami solar panels."

That's why, in 2025, Kuribayashi combined his passion for origami and science to create a simulation program that can predict complex folding outcomes. His research won the $100,000 top prize at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, beating out over 1,700 other high school students from across the globe.

"I still can't believe I took top prize because I have been dreaming about participating in ISEF since I heard of it in eighth grade," he said.

Beauty in nature

Kuribayashi became enamored with origami after his grandmother taught him as a child, but his interest in science didn't crystallize until he became a high school freshman. At the time, an older schoolmate who attended the International Science and Engineering Fair made his passion for the violin the basis of his research.

"My senior analyzed the beauty of the violin, but in my case, what should I analyze? What kind of beauty am I interested in?" Kuribayashi said.

Ultimately, Kuribayashi chose the beauty of nature.

Kuribayashi spent about 6 months developing the simulation program with Julia, a programming language similar to Python. Although he learned how to code in middle school, Kuribayashi said his research was tough. The program uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo, an algorithm that generates sample scenarios and uses them to estimate probable answers.

"I used very difficult algorithms," Kuribayashi said. "I actually participated in a lab at the University of Tokyo. The professor gave me a lot of material that university students use."

Testing the program introduced more hurdles.

"I tested this program a lot of times, but since my programming skills aren't professional, I had all these bugs I needed to fix," Kuribayashi said.

Some people now rely on AI to write code, but Kuribayashi said that the technology can still make mistakes and often requires a human fact-check. So, he opted to do everything himself.

"By analyzing natural origami, which is very efficient, we can take and find a new pattern," Kuribayashi said.

Kuribayashi said new patterns can be used in engineering applications, like creating solar panels that fit into compact spaces and portable emergency shelters.

"Since there are a lot of earthquakes or tsunamis in Japan, we need to make objects that fold into very tiny spaces," Kuribayashi said. "We need to bring shelters really quickly, but shelters need to be very stiff and very big. This is where origami can be used."

A six-figure scholarship

For Kuribayashi, winning the George D. Yancopoulos Innovator Award at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair was a dream. Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and Society for Science hosted the competition, which took place in Arizona this year. The finalists were awarded more than $7 million in prize money.

"I have a lot of appreciation for my family and global teachers. They really helped me to conduct this research," Kuribayashi said. "When I got back from the US, my family and grandparents celebrated. That was really, really nice."

Kuribayashi said he appreciated the opportunity to meet other young people from around the world interested in science.

"I talked with many, many finalists in ISEF," Kuribayashi said. "Local finalists have a huge passion for their research, and that was really, really fascinating. By participating in this kind of international competition, I could interact with new perspectives."

作者：Lauren Edmonds 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

在日本最北端的岛屿上长大的栗林光让自己沉浸在大自然中，那里到处都是折纸图案。

“想象一下一只小瓢虫，”18 岁的栗林告诉《商业内幕》。 “那只瓢虫实际上使用折纸图案来折叠和展开它的翅膀。”

树叶。 花瓣。 昆虫的翅膀。 当他穿越北海道地区广阔的森林和山脉时，他经常会注意到这些复杂的图案。 然而，栗林相信折纸对自然的影响可以超越艺术灵感。

“折纸和连杆已被用于许多其他领域，”栗林说。 “例如，一些在轨卫星使用折纸太阳能电池板。”

这就是为什么在 2025 年，栗林将他对折纸和科学的热情结合起来，创建了一个可以预测复杂折叠结果的模拟程序。 他的研究在 2026 年再生元国际科学与工程博览会上击败了来自全球的 1,700 多名其他高中生，获得了 100,000 美元的最高奖金。

“我仍然不敢相信我获得了最高奖项，因为自从我八年级听说 ISEF 以来，我一直梦想着参加 ISEF，”他说。

自然之美

栗林小时候在祖母教他折纸后就迷上了折纸，但他对科学的兴趣直到高中一年级才显现出来。 当时，一位参加国际科学与工程博览会的老同学将他对小提琴的热情作为他研究的基础。

“我的前辈分析了小提琴的美感，但对于我来说，我应该分析什么呢？ 我对什么样的美感兴趣？” 栗林说道。

最终，栗林选择了自然之美。

Kuribayashi 花了大约 6 个月的时间使用 Julia（一种类似于 Python 的编程语言）开发模拟程序。 尽管他在中学时就学会了如何编码，但栗林说他的研究很艰难。 该程序使用马尔可夫链蒙特卡罗，一种生成样本场景并使用它们来估计可能答案的算法。

“我使用了非常困难的算法，”栗林说。 “我实际上参加了东京大学的一个实验室。 教授给了我很多大学生使用的材料。”

测试该程序引入了更多障碍。

“我多次测试了这个程序，但由于我的编程技能并不专业，所以我遇到了所有需要修复的错误，”Kuribayashi 说。

现在有些人依靠人工智能来编写代码，但栗林表示，该技术仍然会犯错误，并且通常需要人工进行事实检查。 于是，他选择了自己做所有的事情。

“通过分析非常有效的自然折纸，我们可以采取并找到一种新的模式，”栗林说。

Kuribayashi 表示，新模式可用于工程应用，例如制造适合紧凑空间和便携式紧急避难所的太阳能电池板。

“由于日本经常发生地震或海啸，我们需要制造可以折叠到非常小的空间中的物体，”栗林说。 “我们需要非常快地建立避难所，但避难所需要非常坚固且非常大。 这就是折纸可以发挥作用的地方。”

六位数的奖学金

对于栗林来说，赢得了乔治·D· 再生元国际科学与工程博览会上的 Yancopoulos 创新者奖是一个梦想。 再生元制药公司 (Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.) 和科学学会主办了今年在亚利桑那州举行的竞赛。 决赛入围者获得了超过 700 万美元的奖金。

“我非常感谢我的家人和全球老师。 他们确实帮助我进行了这项研究，”栗林说。 “当我从美国回来时，我的家人和祖父母庆祝了。 那真的非常非常好。”

栗林说，他很高兴有机会结识来自世界各地对科学感兴趣的其他年轻人。

“我和 ISEF 的很多决赛入围者进行了交谈，”栗林说。 “当地决赛入围者对他们的研究充满热情，这真的非常令人着迷。 通过参加这种国际比赛，我可以接触到新的视角。”
